episodes.title: GPU Died. Training Didn't: Self-Healing Training at Scale — Crusoe
episodes.description:
Across thousands of GPUs, hardware failures are guaranteed. Fixing them by hand at 3 a.m. doesn't scale.

Connor Guerrero, Young Jeong and Nikhil Gupta from Crusoe explain why they built Managed Slurm on top of Kubernetes. Slurm gives researchers gang scheduling, topology awareness and familiar sbatch workflows, but falls short on dynamic resources, node health and observability. Kubernetes fills those gaps without either team changing how it works. They walk through AutoClusters' fully automatic remediation of an XID 79 GPU failure, then demo killing a GPU mid-training and resuming from checkpoint in under 15 minutes with no human action.

In this talk:
• Where traditional Slurm excels for training and where it falls short
• Why one stack beats separate Slurm and Kubernetes infrastructure
• The automatic remediation flow: notify, drain, replace, requeue, resume
• Sharing GPUs between training and inference as demand shifts

episodes.title: An Interaction Is All You Need — Ivan Leo, Google DeepMind
episodes.description:
Models became agents, and the APIs didn't keep up. Google DeepMind rebuilt them.

Ivan Leo, developer experience engineer at Google DeepMind, introduces the Gemini Interactions API and Managed Agents. He traces how we went from single completions to function calling to agents, then shows server-side state with interaction IDs (no more hand-managing thought signatures), strongly typed multimodal outputs, mixing built-in and custom tools, and the new steps data model. He then demos Managed Agents, which run the Antigravity harness in a persistent remote sandbox with environment IDs, loadable sources, a credential-injecting proxy and named agents, plus the open-source Gemini API CLI.

In this talk:
• Why agent workloads need a different API shape
• Server-side state: interaction IDs and thought signatures
• Chaining image, video and audio generation with the same context
• Managed Agents: persistent sandboxes, skills, secure credentials and named agents

episodes.title: How VS Code Went from Monthly to Weekly Releases with AI — Harald Kirschner
episodes.description:
After 10 years of monthly releases, VS Code now ships weekly. It wasn't more AI that made it work. It was rebuilding the whole system around it.

Harald Kirschner, principal product manager on VS Code at Microsoft, explains how a small team shipping to more than 50 million users moved from monthly to weekly releases with AI agents, and what broke along the way. He covers three stages: shipping faster (agent-ready codebases, skills, TypeScript Go's 10x faster builds, letting agents drive the app), holding quality (mandatory AI code review, AI issue triage, error stacks that turn into auto-fix PRs, staged rollouts) and learning faster (VSC-Bench evals, daily prototyping and smaller squads).

In this talk:
• Code survival: how the share of agent-written code that gets committed rose from 55% to 86%
• Why slow CI compounds when 20 agents hit it at once
• Giving agents a self-correcting loop by letting them use your app
• Turning 51 billion daily telemetry events into auto-filed issues and fix PRs
• Why a 5-character 'hello world' eval cost one model 70x more tokens

episodes.title: Your LLM App Returned 200 OK. It Was Still Wrong. — Marina Petzel, Datadog
episodes.description:
Latency, errors, traffic and saturation tell you your app is up. They don't tell you if it's right.

Marina Petzel, GenAI advocate at Datadog, explains why the classic golden signals are necessary but no longer enough for generative AI applications, and which metrics to add on top. She covers cost monitoring (token creep, model drift, uncached calls and tagging for cost attribution), safety monitoring (prompt injection, PII leakage, toxicity and jailbreaks) and quality monitoring (hallucination rate, relevance, user satisfaction, completeness and RAG retrieval quality).

In this talk:
• Four ways GenAI apps break traditional monitoring assumptions
• Three hidden cost drivers and a four-level tagging strategy
• Safety metrics and the thresholds to aim for
• Five quality metrics, from hallucination rate to RAG retrieval quality

episodes.title: YOLO Mode, Safely: MicroVM Sandboxes for Any Agent — Rowan Christmas, Docker
episodes.description:
Rowan tried to hack himself with his own coding agent. Five prompts later it had found his browser history, his bank accounts and more.

Rowan Christmas, product manager at Docker, shows why harness-level guardrails aren't enough to protect your machine from your own agent, and how microVM sandboxes give you security by design. He demos Docker Sandboxes (sbx): one command spins up an isolated VM with its own kernel, filesystem isolation, secret placeholders, default-deny networking and a full audit trail. It works with Claude Code, Codex or anything else. He also previews agent identity, delegation chains and policy-based governance.

In this talk:
• How a coding agent with default permissions can surface sensitive data on your laptop
• Why microVMs beat harness-level guardrails
• Running any agent in a sandbox with a single command
• Governance: network allow/deny, filesystem rules, MCP catalogs and what's coming next

episodes.title: The 5 Levels of Self-Driving Production — Eric Schwartz, Traversal
episodes.description:
Coding agents made development faster. They also made production a lot harder to debug.

Eric Schwartz, product manager at Traversal, explains why more AI-written code means more time spent troubleshooting, why observability dashboards tell you what broke but not why, and why root cause analysis is a causal problem rather than an observability problem. He lays out five levels of 'self-driving production' and shares case studies on alert intelligence for a PepsiCo supply chain team and incident root cause analysis at American Express. He closes with five questions to ask any AI SRE.

In this talk:
• How coding agents shift engineering time from building to troubleshooting
• Why multi-hop root cause analysis is so hard for humans and LLMs
• The five levels of self-driving production, from war rooms to closed-loop fixes
• Five questions for evaluating an AI SRE

episodes.title: Lessons from Generating 12 Trillion Synthetic Tokens — Bogdan Gaza, DatologyAI
episodes.description:
The web has roughly 30 trillion tokens of usable text. Frontier pre-training needs more. Here's how DatologyAI generates the rest.

Bogdan Gaza, co-founder and CTO of DatologyAI, shares the engineering lessons from running synthetic data jobs at trillion-token scale, including a recent run of about 12 trillion tokens across web, math and code. He covers BeyondWeb, DatologyAI's rephrasing-based synthetic data recipe, and the move from a split Slurm/Kubernetes setup to a single Ray, KubeRay and vLLM pipeline on EKS on HyperPod. He then walks through four bottlenecks: S3 metadata, GPU failures, cross-cluster scheduling and inference tuning.

In this talk:
• Why seeded rephrasing beats asking a model for synthetic data from scratch
• Batching S3 metadata fetches to cut 9–11 days down to about 2 hours
• Right-sized partitions plus checkpointing for recoverable GPU failures
• Scheduling CPU and GPU together across clusters, and vLLM flag sweeps for about 40% more throughput

episodes.title: Why AI Didn't Actually Make You Ship Faster — Gabriel Spencer-Harper, Meticulous
episodes.description:
AI writes code faster than humans can review it. Verification is now your bottleneck.

Gabriel Spencer-Harper, co-founder and CEO of Meticulous, explains why assertion-based tests can't keep up with AI-generated code, and what near-exhaustive frontend verification with zero developer effort looks like. He demos how Meticulous records real user flows, replays them on every pull request and shows visual before/after diffs. He also explains the three technologies that make it work: fully mocked network traffic, a deterministic browser and coverage-guided flow selection.

In this talk:
• Why the space of possible regressions is too big for hand-written assertions
• How record-and-replay visual diffing works on every PR
• Making the browser deterministic to eliminate flaky tests
• Why code coverage finally means 'code tested' when you screenshot every step

episodes.title: Why 99% Accurate Browser Agents Still Fail — Derek Meegan, Browserbase
episodes.description:
A browser agent that's 99% accurate per step succeeds only about 36% of the time over 100 steps. Here's how to beat that math.

Derek Meegan, software engineer at Browserbase, explains what separates a browser-agent demo from thousands of unattended production runs. He covers how agents see the web (text, screenshots and code), why cost builds up with every step while value only comes at the end, and why you should measure success per transaction, not per run. Then he walks through a real architecture for automating a health insurance portal: deterministic tools, OCR verification, pulled-out authentication and skills that keep the agent on the critical path.

In this talk:
• The three ways agents interact with the browser
• Why compounding step risk kills long trajectories, and how retries change the picture
• Performance first, then cost and maintainability as engineering problems
• A production architecture that takes everything deterministic out of the model's hands

episodes.title: Stop Rationing Tokens: Let the Harness Pick the Model — Kimchi by Cast AI
episodes.description:
Token budgets are out of control, and limiting tokens cripples your developers. Cast AI took a different route.

Laurent Gil, co-founder and president of Cast AI, and Žilvinas Urbonas, who leads engineering for Kimchi, show how Cast AI built its own open-source coding harness after its coding-agent bill took off. The key idea is to measure cost per task instead of cost per token, and to let the harness choose the right proprietary or open model for each task based on the outcome. They share three months of internal results with 300 employees, then demo Ferment for multi-hour autonomous tasks, Teleport for agent sessions that keep running after you close your laptop, and Studio for team collaboration.

In this talk:
• Why cost per task matters more than cost per token
• How an outcome-aware harness switches models automatically as new ones ship
• Ferment: milestone-based, self-scoring autonomous coding runs that deploy to staging
• Teleport and Studio: remote sandboxes and a shared Kanban board for agent sessions
